s: to see (something); to perceive by vision
to realize; to notice; to see; to find out
to meet (someone); to meet up; to see; but not in the sense of “pay a visit to”, nor as a euphemism for having a romantic or sexual relation
Do you still see Markus? (Do you meet him regularly? Are you still friends with him?)

to look (at); to watch [with auf (+ accusative) or nach (+ dative) ‘someone/something’]; the construction with nach often implies a turning of the head; other prepositions can be used depending on the context
to check on; to look after; to see to
Hast du in letzter Zeit nach dem Baby gesehen?
Have you seen to the baby recently?
to decide spontaneously and/or by personal preference; to wait and see
We’ll see then. / We’ll play it by ear.
Soll ich Nudeln oder Pizza nehmen? — Das musst du selber sehen.
Should I take pasta or pizza? — You’ll have to decide for yourself.
sehen.et:
From Middle High German sëhen, from Old High German sëhan, from Proto-West Germanic *sehwan.
Compare Low German sehn, Hunsrik sihn, Dutch zien, English see, Danish se, Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌹𐍈𐌰𐌽 (saiƕan), Yiddish זען (zen).

s: Oh, ich hab' solche Sehnsucht / Ich verlier' den Verstand / Ich will wieder an die Nordsee / Ich will zurück nach Westerland

Sehnsucht.et: From sehnen (“to long”) + Sucht (“anxiety; sickness; addiction”).

sehr.et: From Middle High German sēr, from Old High German sēr (“sored, injured”), from Proto-West Germanic *sair. Compare Dutch zeer and English sorely for a similar semantic development.

s: chord, a straight line between two points of a curve
Sehne.et: From Middle High German sën(n)e, sën(e)we, from Old High German senawa, from Proto-West Germanic *sinu, which see. The forms Sehne and Senne alternated widely, though on the whole the former was more northern, the latter more southern.

sehnen.et: Uncertain; compare Middle High German senen (“sadness, grief, heartache”). Has been considered a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-, though whether in the "sow (seed)" or "longlasting" sense is unclear.

sehr gut.et: Univerbation of sehr + gut, literally “very good” as employed informally before being constituted a term of law.
